overview: Carnatic here means the Nawabship of Arcot during the atlas interval from 1783 to 1815, not every Tamil or Telugu community in the wider geographic Carnatic. Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah and Umdat ul-Umara retained a court, titles, correspondence, mints, and revenue claims while East India Company troops, creditors, and officials increasingly controlled war finance and administration. The 1801 treaty transferred exclusive civil and military government to the Company, yet Azim-ud-Daula continued as a titled Nawab with a court and allowance. This card therefore treats 1801 as the decisive political transfer and 1815 as the atlas repaint, not a second conquest. Surviving evidence ranges from treaties, correspondence, debates, coins, and later district histories to Francis Buchanan's 1800 travel observations. It reveals irrigated rice, mud and tiled houses, multilingual learning, court education, smallpox campaigns, debt pressure, and skilled mint work, but unevenly. The polygon is equally imperfect: it includes Arcot and Thanjavur while excluding Company Madras, then disappears into a broad Company layer. People, households, languages, and institutions continued across that cartographic change.

periods.title: 1783 to 1785: war ending and fragile recovery
periods.summary: The atlas begins while the Second Anglo-Mysore War was still ending. The 1784 Treaty of Mangalore concluded the conflict, and revenue administration shifted again in 1785. Raiding, siege, shortage, and competing collectors had weakened both countryside and court, so a painted Carnatic block conceals uneven local recovery.

periods.title: 1785 to 1787: debt and a new Company settlement
periods.summary: Company directors, Madras officials, private creditors, and the Nawab disputed enormous Arcot debts. The 1787 treaty fixed a major subsidy and wartime revenue arrangements. These agreements reduced practical autonomy while leaving Muhammad Ali's court visible, making sovereignty a negotiated and heavily mortgaged relationship rather than a simple border.

periods.title: 1787 to 1790: revenue claims tighten
periods.summary: Debt service and assigned revenues connected court finance to village cultivation. Creditors and revenue farmers sought repayment from land income, while Company oversight expanded. In 1790 another wartime assumption of revenues created a Board of Assigned Revenue, intensifying conflict with hereditary chiefs and cultivators in southern districts.

periods.title: 1790 to 1792: another Mysore war
periods.summary: The Third Anglo-Mysore War again made the Carnatic a military and fiscal corridor. The Company administered revenues during hostilities, then the 1792 settlement revised its relationship with Muhammad Ali. Troop costs, tribute, and collection rights mattered as much as battlefield lines to people supplying grain, cash, transport, and labor.

periods.title: 1792 to 1795: Muhammad Ali's final years
periods.summary: Muhammad Ali remained Nawab until his death in October 1795, but subsidies, creditors, and Company power constrained government. His court sustained correspondence, education, patronage, and coinage amid fiscal strain. The evidence shows neither an independent kingdom untouched by colonial power nor an empty title without institutions.

periods.title: 1795 to 1799: Umdat ul-Umara's court
periods.summary: Umdat ul-Umara succeeded his father in 1795. A catalogued 1796 letter, surviving objections, and coins reveal an active court communicating and minting while Company officials questioned his loyalties. His reign belongs to documentary history, but the surviving archive disproportionately records elite disputes and British administrative concerns.

periods.title: 1799 to 1801: succession and forced transfer
periods.summary: After Tipu Sultan fell in 1799, Company officials used alleged Carnatic correspondence with Mysore to demand control. Umdat died in July 1801. The Company rejected one succession path, installed Azim-ud-Daula, and secured a treaty transferring exclusive civil and military administration on 31 July.

periods.title: 1801 to 1815: titled court, Company government
periods.summary: Azim-ud-Daula retained title, household, and a revenue provision while Company officers governed. Local resistance continued to about 1805, and sepoys at Vellore rebelled in 1806. By 1815 the atlas finally repaints the target as Company territory, fourteen years after the legal transfer.

sections.title: Exact identity, chronology, and atlas geometry

items.text: The exact id is carnatic, indexed approximately from 1783 to 1815 and queued as an Asian state. It has two border files but no exact card, card-index association, researched override, or staged draft. This packet proposes Carnatic Nawabship of Arcot as the clearer display identity.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The exact target appears once in 1783 and once in 1800, matching both coverage intervals with no duplicate or lifetime violation. Its properties run to 1815, although political administration transferred in 1801, so map persistence cannot set the legal chronology.

Both snapshots decode to one identical nondegenerate Polygon with one component, one ring, and fifty-nine positions. The bounding box runs from about 77.49 to 80.48 degrees east and 8.18 to 16.35 degrees north. Identical geometry is editorial reuse, not proof of static surveyed borders.

Arcot, Vellore, Gingee, Cuddalore, Puducherry, Thanjavur, Tiruchirappalli, and Nellore fall inside the tested polygon. Chepauk and Chennai instead belong to the separate madras layer, while Madurai and Seringapatam belong to mysore. The shape therefore cannot mean every place commonly called Carnatic.

The target shares direct topology seams with india, ambur, mysore, madras, golconda, and a Travancore-labeled Netherlands feature in 1783; neighbors change in 1800. At 1815 every sampled target-region point becomes british-east-india-company, and at 1878 British Raj. These are software handoffs, not synchronized population changes.

sections.title: Nawabs, court, Company, and documentary power

items.text: Muhammad Ali Khan Wallajah governed through a court and officers, but Company military support, debt, and control of revenue narrowed his choices. Scholarship describes a successor to Mughal provincial authority becoming dependent on a commercial corporation. Neither the title Nawab nor the word ally by itself measures practical power.

The 1787 settlement required a large annual subsidy and allowed the Company to take most revenues during war. Parliamentary debate later exposed how those terms interacted with private claims. A treaty could preserve ceremonial rank while moving money, soldiers, and enforcement toward Company hands.

British Library catalogues preserve letters between Arcot rulers, Company officials, creditors, and administrators. Tamil Nadu Archives holds related proceedings and manuscripts. Such records prove sustained government and negotiation, yet their survival favors people who wrote, collected revenue, litigated claims, or entered colonial files over quieter household lives.

Umdat ul-Umara's 1796 correspondence and catalogued objections show a ruler answering demands rather than vanishing behind a map label. Company suspicion after 1799 shaped how his actions were recorded. The archive documents accusation and response more securely than it establishes every private intention attributed to him.

The 1801 treaty vested exclusive civil and military administration in the Company and ordered district officers, records, and accounts transferred. Azim-ud-Daula retained rank and provision under the same settlement. This was a forced constitutional transformation, not evidence that the court, family, or regional society ended that day.

sections.title: War, debt, taxation, and local authority

items.text: The Second Anglo-Mysore War brought sieges, requisitioning, disrupted grain movement, and damage to forts and villages before the card opens. Peace in 1784 did not instantly restore fields, credit, or displaced households. The 1783 map freezes a recovery landscape into a confident outline that contemporary administration did not possess.

Arcot debts were secured against fertile districts and collected from land revenue. The resulting burden reached cultivators through rent demands, assignments, and intermediaries, even when loans were contracted at court or in Madras. Financial paperwork at the top could become grain, cash, or arrears demanded in a village.

Private Company servants lent to the Nawab while public officials demanded subsidy payments, creating overlapping interests. Parliamentary scrutiny disputed principal, interest, and legitimacy. For residents, the practical question was often who arrived to collect, what authority they claimed, and whether another collector would arrive after them.

Government district history records that Company revenue management preceded the 1801 cession and that local chiefs resisted afterward until about 1805. Calling the whole polygon Nawab territory hides palaiyakkar authority, negotiated tribute, forts, and armed opposition. Local power did not wait politely for an atlas color change.

Revenue records describe administrators and taxpayers more readily than labor within homes. Archives can trace petitions, accounts, and transfers, but unpaid care, informal bargaining, evasion, and mutual aid often appear only indirectly. Evidence about state extraction should therefore inform daily life without pretending to be a complete household diary.

Francis Buchanan left Madras in April 1800 to investigate agriculture, arts, commerce, customs, and natural history. His first route crossed Conjeveram, Arcot, and Vellore. The survey offers rare near-contemporary observations, although a commissioned traveler saw a route and selected informants rather than every settlement or social group.

Buchanan described a hot, dry plain where irrigated patches near tanks stayed green and rice approached maturity. Rainfall could permit another crop. These details place work, water, and season together, but one journey in April cannot establish annual yields or equal access to reservoirs across the mapped region.

Many roadside homes were mud-built, some neatly tiled and others roofed with palmyra leaves. Materials reflected local resources, cost, repair, and weather rather than one Carnatic house type. The account describes outward appearance; it does not inventory rooms, sleeping arrangements, cooking smoke, ownership, or sanitation inside.

Buchanan called the roads good along his opening route, yet travel still depended on heat, water, animals, carriers, tolls, and political safety. Inns, temples, mosques, markets, and private hospitality could matter at different stops. A passable Company route does not demonstrate easy movement for every traveler.

Arcot municipality remembers the town as an eighteenth-century headquarters of the Nawabs. By this interval the court was closely tied to Chepauk near Madras, which the atlas excludes from Carnatic. Political life therefore connected Arcot, court residences, forts, markets, and Company offices across separate map colors.

sections.title: Food, farming, markets, and skilled work

items.text: Rice fields near tanks show that staple production depended on stored water, rainfall, bunds, channels, seed, draft labor, transplanting, weeding, and harvest. Buchanan observed possible double cropping in favored plots, not universal abundance. War damage, tax demands, and uneven water access could turn the same landscape precarious.

Palmyra leaves appeared on roofs, while cultivated fields and dusty roads framed the opening journey. Households combined farming, transport, repair, food preparation, animal care, and seasonal work in ways the survey only samples. The evidence supports a laboring landscape, but not a single menu or occupation for everyone.

Arcot-style rupees circulated widely in south Indian commerce, and similar designs were copied by other authorities. Coins had to be weighed, recognized, exchanged, and discounted among many issues. Money changers possessed valuable expertise: a pocketful of silver could be purchasing power, a puzzle, or both.

Government Museum metallography found cast copper blanks cold-worked and struck between dies. Irregular shape, weight, and partial legends preserve the craft process as well as official imagery. Mint labor required metal preparation, engraving, repeated hammering, judgment, and quality decisions that ruler lists alone leave invisible.

Wartime shortage and revenue assignment linked food markets to state finance. Merchants, bankers, renters, collectors, soldiers, and cultivators occupied different positions in that chain. High-level debt did not remain abstract when grain lacked buyers, ready money disappeared, or a district's expected revenue had already been promised elsewhere.

sections.title: Households, family, women, and social difference

items.text: Muhammad Ali founded Madrasa-i-Azam for children of the Arcot royal family, and Umdat ul-Umara expanded it. The institution places education inside dynastic household strategy, where relatives, tutors, theologians, attendants, and political succession intersected. It does not show that court opportunities extended equally to ordinary children.

The 1801 arrangement preserved a revenue share for Azim-ud-Daula and the support of his family and court. Later parliamentary debate shows that succession and household provision remained contested. A stipend maintained rank and dependents, but it did not restore civil or military administration.

Mud houses and tiled or palmyra roofs provide evidence for dwellings, not a universal family form. Residents might include spouses, children, elders, servants, lodgers, apprentices, or other dependents. Buchanan's route cannot recover affection, conflict, adoption, inheritance practice, or who controlled each household's resources.

The 1822 to 1825 education survey reported that many girls learned at home and that formal enrollment was strongly uneven. Because this evidence follows Company takeover, it is a nearby benchmark rather than a census for 1783. It still warns against treating school registers as the whole history of learning.

The later survey recorded Brahmin, merchant, Shudra, other-caste, and Muslim pupils in North and South Arcot, with very unequal proportions. It demonstrates social diversity after the transfer, not fixed identities for every earlier resident. Caste, religion, occupation, language, wealth, gender, and locality shaped opportunity differently.

Madrasa-i-Azam's first named head was Moulana Abdul Ali Bahrul Uloom, according to the Government Museum study. Its royal pupils encountered religious and literary learning within a court institution. The surviving notice identifies an elite school and teacher, not a standardized curriculum or attendance record for the wider Carnatic.

In 1822 to 1825, North Arcot returns listed 365 Tamil, 201 Telugu, 40 Persian, and seven English schools, plus other instruction. These figures postdate the card and cannot be copied backward unchanged. They nevertheless show why a Persian-only or Tamil-only picture of regional education would mislead.

The same later survey commonly placed school entry around age five and reported six years or more in North Arcot, with learning also occurring at home. Returns were incomplete and gendered. They provide a nearby administrative snapshot, not a timetable followed by every child under the Nawabs.

Coin production transmitted skills in metal, dies, scripts, weights, motifs, and striking through practice. No consulted source names an apprentice, lesson sequence, wage, or examination inside an Arcot mint. The objects prove skilled learning more securely than they reveal exactly who taught whom beside the anvil.

Persian records, multilingual coins, district accounts, and the 1801 transfer of records reveal specialized literacy among scribes and officials. Tamil, Telugu, Persian, Arabic, and English occupied different settings. Administrative paper does not imply universal reading, and oral instruction remained essential even where written files survive abundantly.

sections.title: Health, medicine, water, waste, and toilets

items.text: In 1787 a Company surgeon at Trichinopoly inoculated European soldiers against smallpox; later efforts included officers' children and some sepoys. Variolation was uncommon in much of the Madras region. These records describe a limited military initiative, not the full range of household care, healers, remedies, childbirth, or disease.

Madras authorities launched a variolation campaign in 1800, publishing material in Arabic, Telugu, and Tamil and asking collectors to encourage participation. By April 1801 they listed 475 inoculations, probably incompletely. Public health depended on translators, local intermediaries, trust, season, and access as much as official orders.

Cowpox vaccine reached Madras late in 1802, after Company government replaced the Nawab's administration. Reported vaccination rose sharply, but supply chains failed and acceptance varied. Women and social groups appeared unevenly in returns. Medical innovation therefore crossed the political transfer without becoming instant or uniformly trusted care.

Buchanan's tanks and reservoirs irrigated nearby rice, but his observation does not establish that people drank directly from them. Water for fields, animals, washing, cooking, and drinking could follow different routes. The consulted route account does not map wells, household storage, drainage, or seasonal water quality.

No consulted period source establishes a household toilet type, sewer network, municipal waste collection, or uniform latrine practice across the Carnatic. Houses, tanks, roads, forts, and health campaigns are documented separately. The card names this evidence gap instead of turning silence in elite and travel records into invented sanitation infrastructure.

sections.title: Languages, writing, coin legends, and art

items.text: Arcot coinage used Persian, Tamil, English, Telugu, Kannada, and Grantha in different issues, while Persian served official court administration. Scripts and motifs varied by denomination, mint, market, and authority. Multilingual money demonstrates communicative choices, not that every user could read every legend crossing a palm.

Written-language sample: سکه مبارک سایه فضل اله حامی دین شاه عالم | سنه ۴ ضرب ارکات جلوس میمنت مانوس. Transliteration: Sikka mubarak saya fazl ilah, hami din Shah Alam; sanah 4, zarb Arkat, julus maimanat manus. Translation: Auspicious coin of Shah Alam, defender of faith, shadow of divine favor; 4, struck at Arcot in a reign of tranquil prosperity.

The sample is a normalized reading of a silver rupee issued by Umdat ul-Umara's Arcot mint in Shah Alam II's name. The standard formula's translation is numismatically documented, but hammered flans may omit letters. The die engraver and original verse author are unknown; attribution belongs to issuer and nominal emperor.

An Umdat ul-Umara gold pagoda paired three deities with the Persian letter ayn. Other Arcot coins combined Islamic names with Hindu figures and local symbols. A tiny coin could carry several political and devotional vocabularies at once, an impressive amount of diplomacy for something easily dropped.

Portraits, Persian manuscripts, letters, and coins preserve court aesthetics and writing. A Library of Congress North Arcot manuscript has uncertain authorship, so it cannot safely become a personal sample for Muhammad Ali. Museum portrait context likewise illuminates representation more securely than the sitter's private character.

The Nawabship sustained a court, diplomatic correspondence, mints, religious patronage, and elite schooling while operating under severe fiscal and military constraint. These were real institutions, even when Company influence penetrated them. Achievement here includes maintaining multilingual administration and cultural production, not claiming unqualified sovereignty or effortless prosperity.

Arcot-style rupees became trusted commercial forms beyond one ruler's territory, while local copper issues used multiple scripts and motifs. That success joined mint craft, market recognition, and political messaging. The variety also created work for money changers, proving that monetary achievement and monetary inconvenience can share the same purse.

Tipu Sultan's defeat in 1799 removed a major regional rival and gave Company officials leverage against Umdat ul-Umara. Nellore's district history records the succession dispute and debt-laden context. Company claims of discovered correspondence remain part of an interested takeover record, not a neutral window into every actor's motives.

On 31 July 1801, Azim-ud-Daula accepted a settlement transferring civil and military government, district records, and policing to the Company. The court continued with title and provision. This precise event is the political ending within the card, even though the atlas preserves the Carnatic polygon until 1815.

The atlas removes carnatic in 1815 and paints all sampled target-region points british-east-india-company. Kancheepuram's government history likewise places Company control in 1801, so 1815 is an editorial endpoint. Families, languages, farming, worship, coin knowledge, and the titled dynasty continued; only the card's mapped layer ends.

ending.text: The card closes at 1815 because the atlas removes the exact carnatic layer and assigns every sampled target-region point to british-east-india-company. The decisive governmental transfer had already occurred on 31 July 1801, when Azim-ud-Daula accepted Company control of civil administration, military affairs, policing, district records, and accounts. He retained title, household provision, and a court, while resistance, negotiation, military service, worship, farming, craft, trade, and family life continued under altered authority. The 1806 Vellore uprising alone shows why the years after transfer cannot be summarized as quiet disappearance. By 1878 the atlas repaints the sampled region again as British Raj. Transformation is therefore the safe ending: the Nawabship lost government in 1801, its court and dynasty persisted, and the map caught up in 1815. No successor association is added because the Company's broad existing record begins long before this transfer and a direct exact-id link would misstate chronology.
